features.title: Features
features.desc: All seven features: battery health, fault codes, live data, system telemetry, inspection reports, sessions and service functions - what each reads and what it needs.

batteryHealth.title: Battery health
batteryHealth.desc: Read state of health and charge, pack voltage, per-cell-group potentials, imbalance and thermal data reported by the vehicle battery management system.

vehicleDiagnostics.desc: ECU discovery over DoIP, identification data, DTCs by status with freeze frames, all-module DID scans, firmware inventory and clearing behind an explicit confirmation.

liveData.title: Live data
liveData.desc: Live engineering telemetry: pack voltage and current, battery and inverter temperature, motor torque and 12 V system voltage, with on-demand periodic sampling.

systemTelemetry.title: System telemetry
systemTelemetry.desc: Subsystem read views beyond the battery: climate loop, drive units, charging and power, TCAM, steering, service schedule, GPS and the vehicle option map.

inspectionReports.title: Inspection reports
inspectionReports.desc: A scored pre-purchase inspection built from read-only diagnostics: pack degradation, cell balance, fault severity and odometer consistency, each verdict traceable to a versioned rule.

sessionsEvidence.title: Sessions and evidence
sessionsEvidence.desc: Diagnostic sessions archive locally and compare inside the app: fault code diffs, cell-by-cell pack history, firmware before and after, operator notes and exports.

about.pIndependence: Hanterill is an independent project. It is not affiliated with, maintained by, sponsored by or authorised by Volvo Cars, Polestar or Geely. Manufacturer and model names are used only to describe which vehicles the software can communicate with. No manufacturer logo is used as a mark of endorsement.
about.pLicense: The source is available to read. Hanterill is provided for personal, non-commercial use under the project license, and is not open source in the OSI sense. The <link>license page</link> has the terms.
about.pWhy: The diagnostic data a modern EV holds about its own battery and drivetrain is detailed and useful, and most of it is readable with standard protocols. Hanterill makes that data available to owners without a proprietary interface or a recurring fee.
about.pFree: Hanterill costs nothing for private use. There is no paid tier, no subscription, no account and no trial, and no diagnostic feature is held back. A workshop that wants to bill for this work can ask about a commercial licence; that option exists so private owners are never charged for it.
about.pHow: The diagnostic engine, DoIP stack and decoders are Rust. The desktop shell is Tauri v2, so there is no bundled browser engine. The interface is React and TypeScript, typed against the engine.
about.pContrib: The most useful contributions are protocol traces, ECU maps and decoder corrections. The repository has the details.

download.pSource: The repository is public and the source is readable, for private and non-commercial use under the project license. Packaged downloads come from the release page. Building from source is not a supported installation path yet.
download.pVerify: Releases are tagged in the repository and publish checksums alongside the binaries. Match the checksum of your download against the one listed on the release page before running it.
download.pCadence: Versions follow SemVer tags. The panel shows the latest published release and its assets; if GitHub cannot be reached it links to the releases page.
download.pHardware: One passive ENET cable and any real Ethernet interface. The cable has no chip in it: OBD-II on one end, RJ45 on the other, wired straight through to the car's diagnostic pins. Everything else is ordinary Ethernet.
download.pBudget: A cable costs a few tens of euros and a USB Ethernet adapter about the same, if your laptop has no port. There is no dongle to buy, no subscription to renew, and no account to create.

stays: Every diagnostic session, DTC read and live capture
never: No crash reporting to a third party
privacy.pVin: The VIN is read as part of vehicle identification. In logs and exports, Hanterill redacts it where it is not required, so a shared session file does not carry a full VIN by default. Per-vehicle caches are keyed by a hash of the VIN.
privacy.pNetwork: During a session, Hanterill communicates only with the vehicle over the local Ethernet link. The website may query the GitHub API to show the latest release; the application itself does not require any internet connection to run.
privacy.pNoSub: Hanterill is free for private use. You do not need an account or subscription to use the desktop app.

safety.pReadOnly: Battery checks, fault scans and live readings ask the car for information. They do not change its configuration. Actions that can change the car are kept in separate flows and require confirmation.
safety.pChanges: Clearing fault codes, running a service routine or resetting a control unit can change the car. Hanterill asks you to confirm each action and reports whether the car accepted it.
safety.pHv: Electric vehicles carry hazardous high-voltage systems. Reading battery data over a diagnostic link does not de-energise anything and does not make physical high-voltage service safe. HV service requires procedures, equipment and training from the manufacturer.
safety.hNoSubstitute: Not a substitute for manufacturer tooling
safety.pNoSubstitute: Hanterill is an independent project. It does not replace the diagnostic system supplied by the manufacturer, and it is not affiliated with Volvo Cars, Polestar or Geely. Use it to understand your vehicle, not as the sole basis for a safety-critical repair decision.
safety.pUnverified: On Testing or Research platforms, the decoding still needs testing on more cars. Do not rely on battery figures or fault interpretation, and do not make purchase or repair decisions from them.

batteryHealth.pWhere: Hanterill reads state of health from the battery controller. Where supported, it also reads learned cell capacity and compares it with the reference for your battery to show capacity loss.
reads: State of health and state of charge
Every cell-group potential on the active pack topology (108 on CMA: 27 modules, 4 groups each)
Minimum, maximum and delta across cell groups
Pack and module temperatures, rendered as a thermal grid
Learned cell capacity compared with the battery's reference, where available
Cross-signal checks: reported pack voltage against the cell sum, reported power against calculated
batteryHealth.pTopologies: Battery layouts differ between models. Hanterill chooses the matching layout so it does not mistake an expected gap for a missing cell group. CMA has the most complete real-car verification; other layouts still need testing on more vehicles.
batteryHealth.pEngineering: Choose Engineering to see more detail about the battery controller and individual readings. The battery guide explains how to interpret them.
batteryHealth.moreSoh: How state of health is read

vehicleDiagnostics.pDiscovery: Hanterill finds the car through the cable, opens a diagnostic connection and checks which control units answer. It remembers units that are not fitted to that car, so later scans do not wait for them unnecessarily.
vehicleDiagnostics.pFaults: The fault list opens on codes that need attention. You can also see older codes, any conditions the car saved with a fault and changes between two scans.
vehicleDiagnostics.pClearing: Clearing requires confirmation. Hanterill can save fault details first, show progress by control unit and scan again afterward to see which codes remain.
vehicleDiagnostics.pDid: The data explorer can read a selected set of values across responding control units. Saved captures can be opened later without reconnecting to the car.
vehicleDiagnostics.pInventory: The inventory lists the hardware and software versions reported by each responding control unit. Compare two saved inventories to see what changed after service or an update. The app also flags mileage readings that disagree.
vehicleDiagnostics.pEvidence: A session exports to JSON or CSV and archives locally. Run one before a repair and one after: the built-in comparison shows fewer codes and fewer active faults. <link>Sessions and evidence</link> covers the comparison views.

liveData.pChannels: Choose the readings you want above the chart. Common battery and drive readings are grouped for a quick start. The refresh rate depends on what the car's control units can provide.
liveData.pReading: Pause the chart to inspect a point. Gaps in the recording stay visible instead of being filled with invented readings. The trace shown here is simulated, not a reading from a car.
liveData.pExport: A running view can be written to CSV for offline analysis.

serviceFunctions.warningLead: None of this happens without your explicit confirmation.
serviceFunctions.warningBody: The actions below can change the car. Hanterill asks you to confirm each one and shows only actions available in the installed app.
routines: Car-wide or per-module clear, with verify re-read
serviceFunctions.pClearing: Before clearing fault codes, you can save the details the car recorded with them. Hanterill then clears the selected control units and scans again to show which codes remain. A separate, optional restart is available for codes that stay latched, but it will not run while the car reports a driving mode. Compare the before and after results in <link>Fault Codes</link>.
serviceFunctions.pAvail: Available routines depend on the car and the installed version of Hanterill. Some are protected by the car's security level. Hanterill can check whether that level is locked, but it cannot unlock it. If the car refuses an action, the app shows the refusal instead of marking it complete.

domains: A single grade composed from the domains below.
State of health read from the BMS, graded against documented bands.
Spread across cell groups on the active topology.
Faults weighted by status and class, not counted flat.
Mileage cross-read across modules; disagreement is its own finding.
inspectionReports.pRules: The report applies documented checks to the readings saved in a session. Open a finding to see what it used. Readings that are still provisional cannot support the strongest verdict on their own.
inspectionReports.pMissing: If the car did not answer, the report marks the reading as missing. Too much missing data makes the overall result inconclusive. Service reminders and other observations may appear as notes without changing the score.
inspectionReports.pReport: The report brings the car's identity, battery, fault and other available findings into a printable document. It shows when missing readings limit the result. You can open a saved session and generate its report again without reconnecting to the car. GPS is left out by default and appears only if you choose to include it.
inspectionReports.pBuying: For a used car, the report brings battery readings, fault history and available mileage checks into one place. It helps you decide what to ask or inspect next. It does not replace a physical inspection. <link>Read how the report is assessed</link>.

pages: Heat pump loop, compressor state, coolant temperatures per loop with the deltas computed, condenser against evaporator.
Front and rear inverter telemetry (IHFA, IEM) with a side-by-side comparison: temperature, voltage, coolant, torque split. A side that did not answer stays empty, never zero.
Socket lock, cable capability, on-board charger state, plus a charge-limitation diagnosis that attributes a capped charge from evidence or declines to.
Charger AC input and DC-DC converter, with the 12 V rail tracked against its state of charge.
Emergency backup-battery health with a length-discriminated layout, raw byte evidence and a digest; GNSS fix only on an explicit button press.
Steering angle sensor: angle, angular velocity, calibration state. Read-only; zeroing is not part of it.
DIM intervals with mileage and time countdowns, and a flag when a counter moves somewhere it should not.
The CEM 256-entry option map with live search, plus the factory build record: anchor VIN, option codes, paint and interior trim.
12 V quiescent current history and module wake-state logs for parasitic-drain chasing.
systemTelemetry.pMeasured: Each field on these pages is a typed observation: value, state, source and decoder version, or a recorded failure. A DID that refuses with a negative response code produces a refusal, not a zero. A parked car with a drifting rotor reading is classified stationary at the display layer without touching the raw value.
systemTelemetry.pChecks: Ten cross-signal checks compare the vehicle's own readings against each other: pack voltage against the sum of its cells, reported power against calculated, current plausibility while parked, compressor state against refrigerant pressure, axle coolant deltas. They run on the live battery, motor and climate reads. A check that is missing an input records it as insufficient data. None of them claims a fault: the worst verdict is a warning.
systemTelemetry.pBoundaries: Cable-rating decoding stays experimental. Option indexes the catalogue does not name remain numeric. Unknown layouts are kept as exploratory evidence rather than turned into a verdict about your car.

diffs: Two scans of the same car: codes added, codes cleared, status changes, snapshot evidence kept.
Two cell lists matched by physical index. A cell populated on only one side keeps a gap, never a zero.
Two inventories compared ECU by ECU: unchanged, software changed, hardware changed, new, missing, unknown.
A stored session re-graded under the current rule version.
sessionsEvidence.pArchive: Hanterill saves sessions on your computer. You can reopen them after restarting the app and add your own notes. The desktop app does not upload them.
sessionsEvidence.pCompare: Choose two saved sessions to see what changed. The comparison can show new or cleared faults, battery readings and software versions side by side.
sessionsEvidence.pReplay: Open a saved capture to inspect it without the car connected. Review a support bundle before sharing it; the export removes identifying details automatically.
sessionsEvidence.pExports: You can save a session or report as a file for your own records. Before sharing it, check whether the vehicle identification number is masked and whether you chose to include location data.
sessionsEvidence.pUsesArchive: The inspection report uses the same archive: <link>scored condition grades</link> re-computable from stored evidence at any time.

pricing.promise: Free for private use, in every release.
pricing.detail: There is no paid tier, no subscription, no account and no trial, and no feature is held back behind one: every diagnostic function the app has is in the download. The licence reserves an optional commercial licence for workshops that bill for this work, so a private owner never pays.
pricing.heading: Private use costs nothing
pricing.body: Hanterill is a tool for owners, not a subscription. It has no paid tier, no account, no trial and no licence server, and no diagnostic feature sits behind one. Private use stays free in every released version.
pricing.commercial: Businesses are the one exception. The licence keeps a commercial option for workshops and service providers, because commercial use is not what CC BY-NC-ND permits. Private owners are unaffected.

features.title: Everything the vehicle will tell you, over one connection.
features.lead: The battery, every ECU, faults, live data, subsystem telemetry and a scored report, read over one connection. No mode switching between tools.
features.batteryBody: State of health and charge, pack voltage, cell-group spread, min, max and delta, and pack temperature. Cross-checks compare reported figures against the measured cells and flag disagreements. The percentage your dashboard shows, and the numbers behind it.
features.scanBody: Hanterill discovers ECUs over DoIP, identifies which speak UDS, and reads the identification, hardware and software data from each. 49 modules in the CMA registry, 40 of them DTC-capable, probed in one pass.
features.faultBody: Hanterill reads DTCs with their status: active now, pending, stored or historical. The list opens on the codes that need attention. If the ECU saved a snapshot when the fault set, you get that too, with a built-in diff between scans.
features.liveBody: Follow battery, motor and 12 V readings as they change. Save the chart when you need to compare it with a later test.
features.systemsTitle: Every subsystem that answers, on its own page
features.systemsBody: Climate loop, drive units with a front-to-rear cross-check, charging plus charge-limit diagnosis, charger and DC-DC power, TCAM backup battery, steering angle, service schedule, GPS on request, and the CEM option map with the factory build record.
features.reportsTitle: A scored health report you can hand to someone
features.reportsBody: The report brings battery condition, cell balance, faults and mileage checks together. It shows when missing readings limit the result.
features.serviceBody: Parking-brake service mode, 12 V battery adaptation, service reminder reset and climate calibration each require confirmation. Some actions may also be protected by the car's security level.
features.evidenceTitle: Before and after, side by side
features.evidenceBody: Sessions archive locally and compare inside the app: fault codes before and after a repair, cell potentials module by module, firmware before and after an update.
features.shellTitle: Built like instrumentation, not like an app
features.shellBody: A command palette, two-key navigation chords, eight themes plus a density setting, eight interface languages, and a full keyboard path through every screen.

platforms.title: CMA tested. SPA partially supported. SEA1 catalogued.
platforms.lead: Polestar 2 and the CMA Volvos are the tested platforms. SPA ships as catalogue data and is partially supported: DoIP connection, module inventory and fault scans have been exercised on a live V90 T6, while hybrid battery reads still need testing on more cars. SEA1 definitions and direct gateway connection are catalogued and still need testing on more cars. Reaching a car is not the same as supporting it.
platforms.disclaimer: Compatibility is not a claim of manufacturer support. Hanterill is an independent project and is not affiliated with Volvo Cars, Polestar or Geely.
platforms.filterEmpty: No vehicles on this platform match that filter.

blurbs.CMA: Compact Modular Architecture. The tested platform: Polestar 2 and the smaller electric Volvos. 108 cell groups, 27 modules by 4. Combustion and hybrid CMA cars are partially supported through the engine reference lane.
blurbs.SPA: Scalable Product Architecture. Partially supported. DoIP connection, module inventory and fault scans have been exercised on a live V90 T6, and the center-tunnel hybrid battery pack layouts ship in the catalogue while deeper battery reads are being verified.
blurbs.SEA: Sustainable Experience Architecture. The SEA1 registry, DoIP routing addresses, DID catalogue and cell mapping for EX30-class cars are defined. The definitions still need testing on more cars.
blurbs.SPA2: Second-generation SPA. Different gateway and security model. Under investigation.

statusNotes.supported: Verified runtime implementation. Battery, DTC, ECU identification and live data are exercised regularly.
statusNotes.partial: Some functions are implemented and verified. Others are not yet covered on this vehicle.
statusNotes.testing: The code is there, but it still needs testing on more cars.
statusNotes.wip: Under active development. It connects, but the decoding is incomplete and changes from release to release.
statusNotes.research: Architecture is being investigated. Not usable for diagnostics.
statusNotes.planned: On the roadmap. No implementation yet.

platforms.serviceModesLead: What the app can actually drive on a car, per service family. Read-only support is exercised on every supported vehicle. Routine support is experimental: the routines exist, they change ECU state, and you run them at your own risk.
platforms.serviceModesNote: Some service actions are protected by the car's security level. Hanterill can check whether a level is locked, but cannot unlock it. A listed action may therefore be refused by your car. Follow the vehicle's service instructions and use these actions only on a vehicle you are authorized to work on. Reading results does not change the car.

service.climate: Climate damper calibration and coolant bleed
service.usage: Gateway usage mode, active and restore

serviceNotes.epb: Retracts the rear calipers for pad or disc work, then clamps and re-learns them.
serviceNotes.steering: Re-learns the straight-ahead reference after steering work. Safety-critical: follow the manufacturer procedure.
serviceNotes.sri: Clears the maintenance-due message and resets the service countdown.
serviceNotes.battery12v: Re-learns the battery sensor after fitting a new 12 V battery.
serviceNotes.tcam: Conditions the emergency backup battery in the telematics module.
serviceNotes.climate: Cycles the blend-door actuators to re-learn their end stops, and runs the coolant bleed pump.
serviceNotes.camera: Re-learns the forward camera, radar and surround-view alignment. Safety-critical: follow the manufacturer procedure.
serviceNotes.sunroof: Re-establishes anti-pinch travel limits after a power loss.
serviceNotes.grille: Re-learns the active grille shutter end stops.
serviceNotes.usage: Sets the gateway usage mode for a diagnostic session, then restores it. The restore step is the safe default.
serviceNotes.dpf: Routine identifiers are not in any recovered data layer, so no build can start a regeneration. Ash, soot and distance read-outs are available.
serviceNotes.aftertreatment: Heater, injector, pump and tank reset identifiers are unrecovered. The urea level read-out is available.
serviceNotes.transmission: Adaptation-mode and clear-adaptation identifiers are unrecovered. Adaptation mileage read-outs are available.
serviceNotes.mildhybrid: Relay unlock and start-disable identifiers are unrecovered. State of charge and state of health read-outs are available.
serviceNotes.generic: Writing values by identifier is refused outright. There is no use case for it and none is planned without a per-operation safety design.

protocolStack.title: Built on automotive standards.
protocolStack.lead: Hanterill talks to the car's diagnostic network with the same protocols a dealer tool uses. Nothing in between is a proprietary cloud service.
protocolStack.paragraph: Hanterill finds the car through the cable, opens a diagnostic connection and sends questions to its control units. Ordinary checks read information. Actions that can change the car are separate and ask for confirmation first.

safety.highVoltageBody: Electric vehicles carry hazardous high-voltage systems. Reading data over a cable does not make it safe to work on them, and Hanterill is not a substitute for the manufacturer's service procedures.

home.q: Do I need a special diagnostic tool or dongle?
home.a: No. A passive ENET cable (OBD-II to RJ45) and any Ethernet interface on your computer are enough for DoIP on supported vehicles. None of the usual OBD dongles are involved.

home.q: Does Hanterill send any data anywhere?
home.a: No. It communicates only with the vehicle and writes results to your disk. There is no account, no backend, no analytics and no telemetry. The VIN is kept out of logs and exports unless something needs it.

Polestar 2 and the CMA-platform Volvos (XC40/EX40, C40/EC40) are the tested platforms. Combustion and hybrid CMA cars are partially supported through the engine reference lane. SPA has provisional DoIP connection, module inventory and fault scans verified on a live V90 T6, while hybrid battery reads still need testing on more cars. SEA1 (EX30, Polestar 4) has battery catalogues and decoders shipping in the app, and direct gateway connection is verified on a Zeekr 001, while battery reads are labelled Testing.

No. Hanterill transmits read services unless you explicitly confirm a write, and every operation that changes the vehicle asks for confirmation on its own under the safety policy. A build compiled without the write feature refuses those commands outright. High-voltage service still requires the manufacturer's procedures.

home.q: Is this an official Volvo or Polestar tool?
home.a: No. Hanterill is an independent project. It is not affiliated with, maintained by or authorised by Volvo Cars, Polestar or Geely. The source is available to read. It is provided for personal, non-commercial use.

home.q: What can I do with the battery data?
home.a: Read state of health and charge, pack voltage, per-cell-group potentials for every populated position (108 on CMA, plus SPA and SEA pack topologies), min/max/delta and pack temperature, and export a session to compare before and after a repair.

home.q: Can I use it without a car?
home.a: Yes. Open a simulated vehicle from the Connection screen to explore the app without a car. Its readings are labeled as simulated and kept separate from real scans. The connection guide explains what you need for a real vehicle.

home.q: What does the inspection report give me?
home.a: The report brings battery condition, cell balance, fault codes and odometer checks into one document. You can review the findings behind its result and create a report from a saved session later. GPS is omitted unless you choose to include it.

compat.q: Does Hanterill work with any Volvo or Polestar?
compat.a: No. Hanterill is CMA-first. Polestar 2 and the CMA Volvos (XC40/EX40, C40/EC40) are the tested platforms. SPA is partially supported: DoIP connection, module inventory and fault scans have been exercised on a live V90 T6, while the hybrid battery path is catalogued and still needs testing on more cars. SEA1 is catalogued and needs testing on more cars. Zeekr, Lynk & Co and SPA2 are Research.

compat.q: What is the difference between platform compatibility and support?
compat.a: Platform compatibility means Hanterill can reach the vehicle over DoIP. Support means the diagnostic functions are implemented and verified against known-good references. Being reachable does not make the data trustworthy, which is why Testing and Research platforms are labelled separately.

compat.q: My car is listed as Partial, Testing or Research. Can I use it?
compat.a: You can connect and, on some, read identification data. Do not rely on battery figures or fault interpretation, and do not run service routines. Partial, Testing and Research all mean the decoding still needs testing on more cars.

compat.q: Is this endorsed by Volvo or Polestar?
compat.a: No. Hanterill is an independent project, not affiliated with, maintained by or authorised by Volvo Cars, Polestar or Geely. Manufacturer names are used only to describe compatibility.

pages.featuresLead: The full coverage, read over the same connection. Standard diagnostics stay read-only; the operations that change the vehicle each ask for confirmation on their own.
pages.batteryHealthTitle: The percentage, and the numbers behind it.
pages.batteryHealthLead: Hanterill reads high-voltage battery data reported by the vehicle: state of health and charge, pack voltage, cell-group distribution, imbalance and temperature, across every pack topology the catalogue knows.
pages.vehicleDiagnosticsTitle: Every ECU on the network, not only the one with the light on.
pages.vehicleDiagnosticsLead: Hanterill discovers the vehicle ECUs over DoIP, identifies which speak UDS, and reads fault, identification and data-identifier content from each.
pages.liveDataTitle: Engineering telemetry on a polling loop.
pages.liveDataLead: Hanterill polls and subscribes to data identifiers and plots them like instrumentation software: fixed axes, thin traces, no decoration.
pages.serviceFunctionsTitle: The operations that change the vehicle stay separate.
pages.serviceFunctionsLead: Where the car and installed app support them, Hanterill can run certain service actions. Each needs its own confirmation. The car may still refuse a protected routine.
pages.inspectionReportsTitle: Before you buy it: a score you can defend.
pages.inspectionReportsLead: Hanterill turns the same reads into a graded pre-purchase inspection, with every verdict traceable to a documented rule.
pages.sessionsEvidenceTitle: The history of the car, kept on your machine.
pages.sessionsEvidenceLead: Sessions archive locally and compare inside the app: fault codes, cell potentials, firmware, before and after.
pages.systemTelemetryLead: Each subsystem with a read path gets its own page: climate, drive units, charging, power, TCAM, steering, service schedule, GPS and the vehicle option map.
pages.vehiclesTitle: CMA tested. SPA partially supported. SEA1 catalogued.
pages.vehiclesLead: Select a platform and a vehicle to see which functions are verified. Each status label reflects what has been checked on that car, not the platform it is built on.
pages.downloadLead: Native builds for each desktop platform. Nothing installs automatically and nothing phones home.
pages.changelogLead: Each tagged build with its notes, newest first, read from GitHub Releases. Versions follow SemVer; the full change history is kept per version.
pages.troubleshootingLead: Work down the list: what to check, in the order that finds the cause fastest, and what the transport does on its own when the link drops.
pages.safetyTitle: What is safe, and what is not.
pages.safetyLead: Diagnostic software can read a great deal and change a few things. Hanterill is built so you always know which is which.
pages.privacyLead: Hanterill has no backend and no account system. It talks to the vehicle and writes to your disk. That is the entire data path.
pages.aboutTitle: A project for people who want to understand their vehicles.
pages.aboutLead: Hanterill started as a way to read CMA battery data without a dealer subscription. It grew into a general DoIP and UDS diagnostic tool.

caseStudy.title: One car, one complaint, start to finish.
caseStudy.lead: A representative session on the reference vehicle: what came in, what the scan found, what the numbers said and what the second scan showed after the repair. Fixed sample data, so every figure below can be checked against the rest of this site.

arrival.title: The car arrives with a complaint
arrival.body: The owner reports that the range estimate dropped further than the weather explains, and that the car charged more slowly than usual on a DC charger twice last month. Nothing on the dashboard. No warning lamp.

scan.title: Connect and identify
scan.body: A passive ENET cable from the OBD-II port to a laptop. Hanterill finds the gateway over UDP 13400, opens a channel on TCP 13400 and activates routing. It then reads the vehicle identification from the gateway and confirms the platform before it asks anything else - the ECU registry, the identifiers and the decoders all follow from that.

codes.title: Read the fault memory
codes.body: Forty-nine control units answer. Three carry codes, and each one is reported with the status byte the module actually stored - not just the code number. That distinction is the difference between an intermittent fault that has already cleared and one that is present right now.

freeze.title: Read the conditions behind them
freeze.body: The BECM saved a snapshot with its code: pack voltage, current, state of charge and temperature at the moment the fault set. The snapshot is what turns a code into a diagnosis - it shows the pack was at 62 % and under load when the module flagged the imbalance, not sitting on a charger.

battery.title: Read the pack itself
battery.body: State of health 94.72 %, cell-group spread 8 mV across 108 potentials, module 14 carrying most of it. The spread is inside tolerance, which is why the car never lit a lamp - and why the dashboard percentage alone could not have told the owner any of this.

verdict.title: Score it
verdict.body: The inspection report scores the session against the rule set it ships with, and cites the rule behind each verdict. The outcome here is a watch item rather than a fault: no code is active, but one module sits at the edge of the tolerance band and the snapshot shows it moving under load.

after.title: Re-scan and diff
after.body: After the module firmware update the workshop applied, a second scan runs and the two sessions compare themselves: which codes cleared, which stayed, which appeared, and how the cell-group spread moved. The archive keeps both, so the comparison does not depend on anyone's notes.

caseStudy.disclaimer: Representative session with sample values. Not a live vehicle reading, and not a diagnosis for any specific car.

troubleshooting.noCarLead: Work down this list in order. The first two cover most cases.

ignition.detail: A sleeping car answers nothing on the diagnostic bus. Turn the ignition on - you do not need to start it, and on an EV there is nothing to start.

port.check: Is the RJ45 end in an Ethernet port?
port.detail: Not a USB-only port on a dock, and not a port that only carries power. The link light on the adapter is the quickest confirmation.

firewall.check: Is a VPN or firewall blocking UDP 13400?
firewall.detail: Discovery is a UDP broadcast on port 13400. A VPN client that captures all traffic, or a host firewall set to block inbound UDP, will stop the car from ever announcing itself. Disable them briefly to test.

adapter.detail: Some cheap USB adapters drop link-local traffic or refuse to come up without DHCP. A direct port on the laptop, or a known-good adapter, rules this out in one step.

exclusive.check: Is another tool holding the connection?
exclusive.detail: One tool talks to the car at a time. Close any other diagnostic software, and give the gateway a few seconds after the last session ends before reconnecting.

troubleshooting.oneCableBody: The cable goes from your computer to the car's diagnostic port, never to your home router, and never to a switch that also reaches your network. Do not bridge the car's network to your normal network.
troubleshooting.dropsLead: Link recovery is built into the transport, so a brief interruption does not cost you the session.

route.label: Route re-activation
route.detail: If the TCP connection drops, Hanterill re-activates the route on the surviving link and carries on with the same session.

stale.label: Stale replies rejected
stale.detail: A reply that arrives on the old connection is discarded as stale, so a late answer cannot be mistaken for a fresh reading.

keepalive.label: Keepalive
keepalive.detail: A TesterPresent every couple of seconds stops the car from putting modules to sleep in the middle of a long sweep.

identity.label: Identity check
identity.detail: If the car reports a different identity after a reconnect, Hanterill ends the session rather than mixing two cars' readings into one file.

troubleshooting.wirelessBody: Some cars expose diagnostics over their own Wi-Fi access point. Where that is available and supported, discovery and routing work the same way over the wireless interface. The wired path is the tested one.
troubleshooting.figureCaption: Adapters that work, and the ones that do not
troubleshooting.stillStuck: Still stuck? The connection reference has the full protocol detail, and the network explorer shows what should be answering.

works: A passive ENET cable: OBD-II on one end, RJ45 on the other. No chip, no firmware, no driver.
The built-in Ethernet port on a laptop, when it has one.
A USB-C or Thunderbolt Ethernet adapter from Apple, Belkin, Anker, UGREEN, Dell or Lenovo.
A USB-A Ethernet adapter with an ASIX AX88179 or Realtek RTL8153 chipset.
avoid: ELM327 and other generic OBD-II dongles. They speak a serial protocol, not DoIP.
J2534 pass-through interfaces. They are for manufacturer flash tools, not for standard DoIP.
Any adapter that presents itself as a serial port rather than a network interface.
A router or switch between the laptop and the car.
adapters.why: The test is whether the adapter gives the operating system a real network interface. If it appears as a serial port, or if it terminates the link itself, Hanterill cannot reach the car through it.

home.moreLead: Every instrument on this page has a full page behind it. The walkthrough takes each feature in turn; the case study follows one session from complaint to verified repair.
